q-105136.name: Question 1
q-105136.problem:
Let $V=C[-\pi ,\pi ],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,g(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t)}$ equals $5\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$
q-105136.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{2}(t)}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{2}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(t){f}_{2}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =5{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t-4{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is an odd function, while $\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is even. Hence, their product $\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =-4{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) & =\frac{-4{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =\frac{-4{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Let V=C[−π,π], the vector space of continuous functions over [−π,π], and let the inner product on V be defined as ⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=∫−ππx(t)y(t)dt.

Now consider the following elements of V:

f1(t)=cos⁡t,f2(t)=sin⁡t,g(t)=5cos⁡t−4sin⁡t+1

Find the orthogonal projection of g(t) onto S=Span{f1(t),f2(t)} given that f1(t)⊥f2(t) with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of g(t) onto Span{f1(t)} equals 5cos⁡t.

a
5cos⁡t−4sin⁡t
b
cos⁡t−sin⁡t
c
5cos⁡t−4sin⁡t+1
d
5cos⁡t+4sin⁡t+1
e
4cos⁡t+5sin⁡t+1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the set {f1(t),f2(t)} is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of g(t) onto the subspace S is given by

projSg(t)=projf1(t)g(t)+projf2(t)g(t).

We are given that projf1(t)g(t)=5cos⁡t, so let's now find the orthogonal projection of g(t) onto Span{f2(t)}. This can be computed as

projf2(t)g(t)=⟨g(t),f2(t)⟩⟨f2(t),f2(t)⟩f2(t).

In our case, we have

⟨g(t),f2(t)⟩=∫−ππg(t)f2(t)dt=∫−ππ(5cos⁡t−4sin⁡t+1)⋅sin⁡tdt=5∫−ππcos⁡tsin⁡tdt−4∫−ππsin2⁡tdt+∫−ππsin⁡tdt

Notice that sin⁡t is an odd function, while cos⁡t is even. Hence, their product cos⁡tsin⁡t must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval [−π,π], which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

∫−ππcos⁡tsin⁡tdt=∫−ππsin⁡tdt=0.
So, we have ⟨g(t),f2(t)⟩=−4∫−ππsin2⁡tdt.

Therefore,

projf2(t)g(t)=−4∫−ππsin2⁡tdt⟨f2(t),f2(t)⟩⋅sin⁡t=−4∫−ππsin2⁡tdt∫−ππsin2⁡tdt⋅sin⁡t=−4sin⁡t.

Finally,

projSg(t)=projf1(t)g(t)+projf2(t)g(t)=5cos⁡t−4sin⁡t.

q-105186.name: Question 2
q-105186.problem:
Let $V=C[-\pi ,\pi ],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=2,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,g(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t+6
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t)}$ equals $6.$
q-105186.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=6,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{2}(t)}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{2}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(t){f}_{2}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t+6)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t-2{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t+6{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is an odd function, while $\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is even. Hence, their product $\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have integrals over the interval $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =-2{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) & =\frac{-2{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =\frac{-2{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =6-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2

Let V=C[−π,π], the vector space of continuous functions over [−π,π], and let the inner product on V be defined as ⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=∫−ππx(t)y(t)dt.

Now consider the following elements of V:

f1(t)=2,f2(t)=sin⁡t,g(t)=cos⁡t−2sin⁡t+6

Find the orthogonal projection of g(t) onto S=Span{f1(t),f2(t)} given that f1(t)⊥f2(t) with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of g(t) onto Span{f1(t)} equals 6.

a
2−sin⁡t
b
8+sin⁡t
c
4+2sin⁡t
d
6−2sin⁡t
e
1−sin⁡t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since the set {f1(t),f2(t)} is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of g(t) onto the subspace S is given by

projSg(t)=projf1(t)g(t)+projf2(t)g(t).

We are given that projf1(t)g(t)=6, so let's now find the orthogonal projection of g(t) onto Span{f2(t)}. This can be computed as

projf2(t)g(t)=⟨g(t),f2(t)⟩⟨f2(t),f2(t)⟩f2(t).

In our case, we have

⟨g(t),f2(t)⟩=∫−ππg(t)f2(t)dt=∫−ππ(cos⁡t−2sin⁡t+6)⋅sin⁡tdt=∫−ππcos⁡tsin⁡tdt−2∫−ππsin2⁡tdt+6∫−ππsin⁡tdt

Notice that sin⁡t is an odd function, while cos⁡t is even. Hence, their product cos⁡tsin⁡t must be an odd function. Now, since we have integrals over the interval [−π,π], which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

∫−ππcos⁡tsin⁡tdt=∫−ππsin⁡tdt=0.
So, we have ⟨g(t),f2(t)⟩=−2∫−ππsin2⁡tdt.

Therefore,

projf2(t)g(t)=−2∫−ππsin2⁡tdt⟨f2(t),f2(t)⟩⋅sin⁡t=−2∫−ππsin2⁡tdt∫−ππsin2⁡tdt⋅sin⁡t=−2sin⁡t.

Finally,

projSg(t)=projf1(t)g(t)+projf2(t)g(t)=6−2sin⁡t.

q-105416.name: Question 3
q-105416.problem:
Let $V=C[-\pi ,\pi ],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,g(t)={sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{2}(t)}$ equals $-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$
q-105416.worked_solution:
Since the set ${{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{{f}_{1}(t)}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{1}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }g(t){f}_{1}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ is an odd function, while ${sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is even. Hence, their product $\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{0}{⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{1}(t)⟩}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t=0.
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =0-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

∫−ππsin⁡t(sin2⁡t−cos⁡t)dt=0.

projf1(t)g(t)=0⟨f1(t),f1(t)⟩⋅sin⁡t=0.

q-105461.name: Question 4
q-105461.problem:
Let $V=C[0,1],$ the vector space of functions that are continuous over $[0,1].$ Given that the inner product on $V$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

find the distance between $f(t)=3t$ and $g(t)=-3t+3$ with respect to the inner product.
q-105461.worked_solution:
The distance between $f(t)=3t$ and $g(t)=-3t+3$ with respect to the given inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖f(t)-g(t)‖ \\  & =‖3t-(-3t+3)‖ \\  & =‖6t-3‖ \\  & =\sqrt{⟨6t-3,6t-3⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨6t-3,6t-3⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6t-3)^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(36{t}^{2}-36t+9)\text{d}t \\  & =[12{t}^{3}-18{t}^{2}+9t]_{0}^{1} \\  & =(12-18+9)-0 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the distance is $d=\sqrt{3}.$

q-105475.problem:
Let $V=C[0,1],$ the vector space of functions that are continuous over $[0,1].$ Given that the inner product on $V$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

find the distance between $f(t)=8t$ and the subspace spanned by $g(t)=4t-2$ with respect to the inner product.
q-105475.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $f(t)$ onto $\text{Span}{g(t)}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{g(t)}\,f(t) & =\frac{⟨f(t),g(t)⟩}{⟨g(t),g(t)⟩}\,g(t) \\  & =\frac{{\int }_{0}^{1}8t\cdot (4t-2)\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{0}^{1}(4t-2)^{2}\,\text{d}t}\cdot (4t-2) \\  & =\frac{{\int }_{0}^{1}(32{t}^{2}-16t)\,\text{d}t}{{\int }_{0}^{1}(16{t}^{2}-16t+4)\,\text{d}t}\cdot (4t-2) \\  & =\frac{[\frac{32}{3}{t}^{3}-8{t}^{2}]_{0}^{1}}{[\frac{16}{3}{t}^{3}-8{t}^{2}+4t]_{0}^{1}}\cdot (4t-2) \\  & =\frac{(\frac{32}{3}-8)-0}{(\frac{16}{3}-4)-0}\cdot (6t-3) \\  & =\frac{(\frac{8}{3})}{(\frac{4}{3})}\cdot (4t+2) \\  & =2\cdot (4t-2) \\  & =8t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

The distance between $f(t)=8t$ and the subspace spanned by $g(t)=4t-2$ with respect to our inner product is

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =‖f(t)-{\text{proj}}_{g(t)}\,f(t)‖ \\  & =‖8t-(8t-4)‖ \\  & =‖4‖ \\  & =\sqrt{⟨4,4⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨4,4⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4\cdot 4\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}16\,\text{d}t \\  & =16t\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =16-0 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the distance is $d=\sqrt{16}=4.$
